conversation.content:
Hello—thank you so much for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Reed, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into life with your new baby.

We’re going to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s a quick way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally during the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays confidential within our care team. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause.

I’ll ask ten questions, one at a time, in everyday language so we can keep things conversational. When you’re ready, we’ll start.

Over the past week, what moments—if any—have brought you joy or laughter, and how often would you say that happened?
Honestly… I can’t think of many. I smiled when the baby wrapped her hand around my finger while she was nursing, but it didn’t last long. Most of the time I just feel tired and flat.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… maybe once or twice when my partner made a silly joke, but even then the laugh felt kind of forced and faded fast. Mostly I’m just too worn-out to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited about little outings—like taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend—but when the time comes I just feel “meh.” I still go, and part of me hopes it’ll lift my mood, but the spark isn’t really there anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she was fussy for hours and I kept thinking it must be something I ate, or that I’m just not soothing her right. Rationally I know babies cry, but I still feel like I’m failing her sometimes.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly at night. I’ll lie there listening to every tiny grunt she makes, convinced something’s wrong even when she’s perfectly fine. My heart races and I can’t settle unless I get up and check her breathing—again. I know it sounds silly, but I can’t shake the worry.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times, yeah. It’s usually when she’s finally asleep and the house is quiet—suddenly my chest gets tight, my mind jumps to “what if she stops breathing?” and I feel like I have to run in there right away. It passes after a minute, but it’s scary while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, definitely. When she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up and I can’t even find time to shower, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. I usually get through it, but I end up exhausted and snapping at my partner over nothing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly unhappy—more like my mind won’t turn off. I lie down and start replaying every little thing I did that day: Did I burp her long enough? Was that rash normal? Then I’m wide-awake for an hour or two, even when the baby’s out cold.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yeah… I get waves of it, especially in the evenings. It’s not all day, but most nights I end up tearing up for no clear reason—just feeling heavy and like I’m missing something I can’t name.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a few times this week, but not every day. It’s usually when I’m feeding her in the middle of the night and the house is so quiet—I just feel overwhelmed and the tears come. They stop pretty quickly, but it still catches me off-guard.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I get tired and weepy, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel like me again so I can be the mom she deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 20: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (2 wks postpartum):
- Persistent low mood, evening tearfulness, sense of “heaviness”
- Markedly reduced pleasure/interest in usual activities (anhedonia)
- Excessive self-blame and guilt about parenting adequacy
- Significant nocturnal anxiety with somatic arousal (racing heart, chest tightness) and intrusive catastrophic thoughts re: infant safety
- Episodic panic symptoms occurring when infant asleep, relieved only by checking
- Frequent rumination interfering with sleep onset independent of infant care demands
- Daily feelings of being overwhelmed; irritability toward partner
- No self-harm ideation; protective of infant

Pattern: Meets clinical threshold indicators for possible postpartum depression ± comorbid postpartum anxiety. Key red flags—mood-congruent insomnia, anhedonia, pathologic guilt, panic-equivalent episodes. Safety screen negative for self-harm.

Recommendation: Elevated risk; refer for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation and evidence-based intervention.
